The tradeoff is sensitivity. A low threshold catches more attacks but floods analysts with false positives, causing alert fatigue where real alerts get ignored. A high threshold keeps the queue quiet but risks false negatives, letting slow or quiet attacks pass. We tune using context and known-benign exceptions, and we accept the SIEM is only as good as its coverage: a system that isn't sending logs is a blind spot.
rubricPoints: Telemetry from many sources is collected centrally in a SIEM.
Normalization puts data into common fields and a single time reference.
Correlation links separate events into one meaningful pattern.
Baselines or behavior analytics detect deviations from normal.
Sensitivity trades false positives and alert fatigue against false negatives.
Missing log sources create blind spots.

suggested.rationale: Investigating failed SSH logins makes the learner sift raw authentication logs and recognize the failure-then-success pattern that correlation rules are built on.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Health Analytics: One Company, Three Rulebooks
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Health Analytics is a fictional US company of about 600 staff. It runs a cloud-hosted claims-processing platform, which is software that hospitals use to send insurance claims containing patient names, diagnoses and treatment details. Hospitals pay Brightwater a monthly subscription by credit card, and Brightwater currently stores full card numbers in its own database so it can charge them each month. Next quarter Brightwater will start serving hospitals in Germany and France, so it will begin holding personal data about people in the European Union (EU).

Three sets of rules now apply. HIPAA (the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) is a US law that protects identifiable health information held by healthcare providers, insurers and the companies that handle that data for them. GDPR (the General Data Protection Regulation) is an EU law that protects personal data about people in the EU, wherever the company holding it is based. PCI DSS (the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) is a contract-based security standard that card brands require of any business that stores, processes or sends card data. It is not a law, but breaking it can cost a business fines or its ability to accept cards.

Backups go to CopperVault, a third-party backup vendor (an outside company providing a service). CopperVault quietly uses a subprocessor, which is a further company that handles the data on CopperVault's behalf, located in a country outside the EU. Brightwater's contract with CopperVault has no security clauses and no right to audit.

The risk register, which is the document listing each known risk with its owner, likelihood, impact and chosen response, contains these entries. Risk A: full card numbers stored in Brightwater's own database. Risk B: theft of staff laptops, which are already encrypted. Each theft has a single loss expectancy (SLE, the cost of one occurrence) of $5,000, and the annual rate of occurrence (ARO, how many times a year it is expected) is 2. A proposed tracking-and-remote-wipe service would cost $30,000 per year. Risk C: ransomware (malware that encrypts data and demands payment) taking down the claims platform. Risk D: an old fax-to-email intake system that receives about 10 claims a month, is no longer supported by its maker and cannot be patched.

For business continuity, the claims platform is the critical system. Leadership says it can be down for at most 4 hours. Contracts with hospitals say Brightwater must never lose more than 15 minutes of submitted claims. Today the platform is backed up once a night to CopperVault, and a full restore has been tested at 12 hours.

1. For each of HIPAA, GDPR and PCI DSS, say why it applies to Brightwater and give one concrete obligation it creates.
2. For Risks A to D, choose a risk treatment (avoid, mitigate, transfer or accept) and justify it. For Risk B, calculate the annualized loss expectancy and use it in your decision. Say who should formally sign off any accepted risk.
3. List the changes Brightwater should make to manage the third-party and supply-chain risk from CopperVault and its subprocessor.
4. State the recovery time objective and recovery point objective for the claims platform, explain whether the current setup meets them, and propose an architecture that would.
modelAnswer: HIPAA applies because Brightwater handles identifiable health information on behalf of hospitals (covered entities), which makes it a business associate, meaning an outside company that handles health data for a covered entity. Acceptable obligations include: sign a business associate agreement (a contract setting out how the health data must be protected) with each hospital, and pass equivalent terms down to CopperVault; apply administrative, physical and technical safeguards such as access control, audit logging and encryption; notify the hospitals of breaches. GDPR applies because Brightwater will process personal data, including health data, about people in the EU. Health data is a special, more sensitive category under GDPR. Acceptable obligations include: have a lawful basis for processing; sign a data processing agreement (a contract that binds a processor to the controller's instructions and security terms) and approve any subprocessors; protect transfers of EU data to countries outside the EU with an approved legal mechanism such as standard contractual clauses (pre-approved EU contract terms for data transfers); report qualifying breaches to the regulator within 72 hours; honour data-subject rights such as access and erasure. PCI DSS applies because Brightwater stores card numbers. Acceptable obligations include: protect stored card data with strong encryption or not store it at all, restrict access to card data, segment the card environment from other systems, and complete regular compliance validation. A full answer notes that PCI DSS is contractual, not a law, while HIPAA and GDPR are laws.

Risk A: avoid. Stop storing full card numbers by using a payment processor that tokenizes cards, meaning it returns a stand-in value that is useless to a thief, so Brightwater can still charge monthly. This removes the data and shrinks PCI DSS scope. Describing it as transferring the risk to the processor, combined with avoiding storage, is also acceptable. Risk B: annualized loss expectancy (ALE) = SLE x ARO = $5,000 x 2 = $10,000 per year. The proposed control costs $30,000 per year, three times the expected loss, so the best answer is accept. The laptops are already encrypted, which lowers the impact. Risk C: mitigate, with controls such as immutable or offline backups (copies that cannot be altered or deleted for a set period), endpoint protection, network segmentation, patching and multi-factor authentication. Transfer some of the financial impact with cyber insurance. Mitigate plus transfer together is the strongest answer. Risk D: avoid, by retiring the unpatchable fax system and moving its roughly 10 claims a month to the supported platform, because the business value is small and the exposure is ongoing. Sign-off: an accepted risk must be formally approved and recorded in the risk register by an accountable business risk owner or executive, such as a senior executive or the risk committee, within the organisation's risk appetite (the level of risk leadership has agreed to tolerate). It should be reviewed periodically. The engineer who found the risk should not approve it alone.

Strong answers include most of the following. Perform due diligence and a vendor risk assessment of CopperVault, for example security questionnaires, independent audit reports and certifications. Renegotiate the contract to add security requirements such as encryption in transit and at rest, breach notification within a set time, a right to audit, data return and deletion at contract end, and the flow-down of HIPAA business associate terms and GDPR data processing terms. Require CopperVault to disclose all subprocessors and get Brightwater's approval before using new ones. Confirm a lawful GDPR transfer mechanism for the non-EU subprocessor, such as standard contractual clauses plus a transfer risk assessment, or require EU-located storage. Have Brightwater encrypt backups before they leave its environment and hold the keys itself. Add CopperVault and its subprocessor to the risk register and inventory, with an owner. Set up ongoing monitoring and periodic reassessment rather than a one-time check. Include an exit or alternative-provider plan to avoid depending on a single vendor. The key idea is that Brightwater stays accountable for the data even when an outside party holds it, so risk must be managed across the whole chain, not just with the direct vendor.

The recovery time objective (RTO), the maximum acceptable time to restore the service after a disruption, is 4 hours. The recovery point objective (RPO), the maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time, is 15 minutes. The current setup fails both. Nightly backups mean up to about 24 hours of claims could be lost, far beyond 15 minutes, and the tested 12-hour restore exceeds the 4-hour RTO. A suitable design replicates data continuously or near-continuously, for example database replication or log shipping every few minutes, so the RPO is 15 minutes or less. It keeps a standby environment, a warm or hot site (a secondary location kept partly or fully running), in a separate region or availability zone, able to fail over in under 4 hours. Answers should also keep immutable or offline backups as a separate layer, because replication will also copy ransomware damage or deletions. Data replicated to the standby site must stay within allowed locations for GDPR. Finally, the business continuity and disaster recovery plan should be documented and tested regularly, through tabletop exercises and real failover tests, so the 4-hour and 15-minute targets are proven rather than assumed.

scenarios.title: Redesigning Harrowgate Freight's Flat Network for Zero Trust
scenarios.scenario:
Harrowgate Freight is a fictional mid-sized logistics company with 1,200 staff, 300 outside contractors, and a head office plus 14 depots. Its security design dates from about 2012 and is now being reviewed.

Today, remote workers and contractors connect through a VPN (virtual private network, an encrypted tunnel that places a remote laptop onto the internal network as if it were in the office). Once connected, they can reach almost everything, because the internal network is flat. A flat network is one big network segment with no internal barriers, so any device can talk to any other device. The billing servers, which handle customer card payments, sit on that same flat network next to depot printers and staff laptops.

All accounts live in one on-premises directory. A directory is the central database of user accounts and passwords. Contractors get full staff accounts, and nobody removes those accounts when contracts end. Logins use a password only.

A shared file server holds everything in one large folder tree: customer contracts, staff salary spreadsheets, card payment exports, and public marketing brochures. Every staff member and contractor can read it. Data on it is not encrypted, and nothing tracks what is copied off it.

The company is also moving its shipment-tracking application to a public cloud provider. This creates a hybrid setup, meaning some systems stay on premises and some run in the cloud.

Leadership has asked you to redesign the architecture using Zero Trust. Zero Trust is a security model that never trusts a user or device just because it is inside the network. Instead, every request is checked against identity, device health, and context, and is given only the minimum access it needs.

For each task below, state your design and defend at least one tradeoff it creates.

1. Explain which Zero Trust principles the current remote access and flat network break. Then propose a replacement for the VPN that works for staff and contractors reaching both on-premises and cloud applications.
2. Design network segmentation for the billing servers and the depot devices, including where microsegmentation fits.
3. Redesign identity and access management for staff and contractors, covering how users prove who they are and how contractor access is controlled over its whole life.
4. Design a data security approach for the shared file server, covering classification, protection, and what happens to data at the end of its life.
subParts: Zero Trust gaps and VPN replacement
modelAnswer:
The current design breaks several Zero Trust principles. The first is implicit trust based on location: once a laptop is on the VPN, the network treats it as trusted and lets it reach almost anything. Zero Trust says network location should grant no trust. The second is least privilege, which means giving each user only the access their job needs. A contractor who needs one app can currently reach billing servers. The third is continuous verification: the user is checked once at VPN login and never again, and the health of the device is never checked. The fourth is assume breach, which means designing as if an attacker is already inside. On a flat network, one infected laptop can move sideways to any server. That sideways movement is called lateral movement.

The replacement is Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA). ZTNA is a broker that connects a verified user to one specific application, never to the whole network. Each request is checked against identity, multifactor login, device posture (is the laptop patched, encrypted, and running endpoint protection), and context such as location and time. The applications are hidden from the internet and are only reachable through the broker.

ZTNA can be delivered as part of SASE (Secure Access Service Edge). SASE is a cloud-delivered service that combines ZTNA, web filtering, a cloud firewall, and data loss controls at points of presence close to users. Because of that, staff and contractors get the same policy whether the application is in the head office, a depot, or the public cloud. Worked example: a contractor opens the tracking app. The broker checks their identity and multifactor login, then confirms the laptop is compliant. The broker then opens a session to the tracking app only, so the billing servers stay invisible to that contractor.

Tradeoffs to defend. First, migration effort: every application must be published individually and given its own access policy, so a phased rollout is needed, with the VPN kept briefly for unmigrated legacy apps. Second, contractor devices the company does not manage may fail posture checks. The answer is to offer browser-only, agentless access with download blocked, rather than full access. Third, dependence on the SASE provider's availability, which is mitigated with contractual uptime commitments and a documented fallback plan.

Split the flat network into segments by function and trust level, enforced by firewalls or access rules between segments. Suggested zones are: a billing/payment zone, a general server zone, a staff user zone, a depot device zone for printers and scanners, a management zone for administrator tools, and a guest zone. The default rule between zones is deny. Only the specific flows that are needed are allowed. For example, depot printers may reach the print server only, and users may reach billing only through the billing application's front end, never directly.

Microsegmentation is fine-grained segmentation applied at the level of individual workloads (a server, virtual machine, or container). Rules are usually enforced by a host agent or the hypervisor, and they follow the workload's identity or labels rather than its IP address. Use it inside the billing zone so that even billing servers can only talk to each other on the exact ports required. Also use it in the cloud tracking app, using the provider's security groups, which are per-workload firewall rules, so each tier talks only to the tier next to it.

Worked example: malware lands on a depot printer. Under the old design it could scan for and reach the billing servers. Now the depot zone rules allow only the print server, so the attempt is blocked and logged, and the problem stays contained.

Why this matters for billing: shrinking the card-data environment to one tightly controlled zone reduces both exposure and the scope of payment-card compliance audits.

Tradeoffs to defend. First, there is more rule management and a risk of breaking legitimate traffic. The mitigation is to map the real traffic flows first, run the rules in monitor mode, and then enforce them. Second, microsegmentation agents add overhead and may not support old systems. Legacy devices that cannot run agents are protected by coarser zone-level firewall rules instead. Third, more segments mean harder troubleshooting, so central logging of allowed and denied flows is required.

Move to a central identity provider (IdP), the service that authenticates users and issues trusted login tokens to applications. Connect the on-premises directory to it so the directory and cloud apps share one identity. That lets one account work across on-premises and cloud apps. Use single sign-on (SSO), meaning one verified login gives access to many apps, and federation, meaning applications trust tokens issued by the IdP instead of keeping their own passwords.

Require multifactor authentication (MFA), where a login needs two or more different kinds of proof, such as a password plus a phone prompt or hardware key. Prefer phishing-resistant methods such as hardware security keys for administrators and billing staff.

Add conditional access, which means policies that decide at login time whether to allow, block, or demand extra proof, based on user, device health, location, and risk. For example: billing access requires a compliant company device and a hardware key.

Apply least privilege through role-based access control (RBAC). In RBAC, permissions are attached to job roles and users get roles, never one-off grants. Separate privileged accounts from daily accounts. Use privileged access management (PAM) for administrators, which means admin rights are granted just in time for a limited period, approved, and recorded.

For contractors, the lifecycle is called joiner-mover-leaver. Contractors get separate contractor accounts, not full staff accounts. Each account has a sponsor (a named employee), a role limited to the apps the contract needs, and an expiry date that matches the contract end. Accounts are disabled automatically at expiry unless the sponsor renews. Quarterly access reviews require sponsors to confirm each contractor still needs access. Ideally, contractor accounts are created from the vendor's own identity system through federation, or from an HR or vendor-management record, so that ending the contract triggers removal.

Worked example: a contractor's term ends on 30 June. On 1 July the account is disabled automatically, their sessions are revoked, and the sponsor is notified. No orphaned account is left behind for an attacker to reuse.

Tradeoffs to defend. First, MFA and conditional access add friction, so use SSO to reduce the number of logins, and use risk-based prompts rather than constant ones. Second, centralizing on one IdP creates a single point of failure and a high-value target. Mitigate this with provider redundancy, break-glass emergency accounts stored securely, and strong protection of IdP administrators. Third, expiry dates can cut off a contractor whose work runs late, so the sponsor renewal step must be simple and fast.

Start with data classification, which means labelling data by how harmful its exposure would be, so that protection matches value. Example levels: Public (marketing brochures), Internal (general operations documents), Confidential (customer contracts), and Restricted (salary data and card payment exports). Data owners, meaning the business managers responsible for each data set, assign the labels. Automated discovery tools scan the share to find card numbers and salary data so that sensitive files that were missed get labelled.

Next, restructure storage by classification. Move Restricted and Confidential data out of the open folder tree into separate locations whose access follows the RBAC roles. For example, salary data goes to HR only, and card exports go to billing only. Ideally, card exports are reduced or tokenized. Tokenization replaces card numbers with meaningless substitutes, so less real card data is stored at all.

Protection controls are as follows. Encryption at rest means stored data is scrambled so stolen disks or backups are unreadable without the key. Encryption in transit, such as TLS, protects data moving across the network. Keys are kept in a managed key service or hardware security module, separate from the data, with access to keys restricted. Data loss prevention (DLP) is a set of tools that spot labelled or sensitive data and block or alert when someone tries to send, upload, or copy it outside approved paths; it can be enforced through the SASE service as well as on endpoints. Logging records who opened or copied Restricted files.

Lifecycle covers creation, storage, use, sharing, archiving, and destruction. Each class gets a retention period. For example, card exports are kept only as long as needed, then securely deleted. Expired data is destroyed by crypto-shredding (destroying the encryption key so the data becomes unreadable) or by secure wiping, including copies in backups and in the cloud.

Worked example: a user tries to upload a payment export to a personal cloud drive. The file carries the Restricted label, so DLP blocks the upload, logs it, and alerts security.

Tradeoffs to defend. First, classification takes effort and depends on people labelling correctly. Mitigate this with default labels, automated discovery, and short training. Second, DLP can produce false positives that block real work, so start in alert-only mode and tune before blocking. Third, encryption makes key management critical: lose the keys and you lose the data. Fourth, shorter retention lowers breach exposure but must still meet legal and tax record-keeping requirements, so retention periods are agreed with the data owners and legal.

scenarios.title: Securing a Smart Warehouse Rollout at Harrowgate Cold Storage
scenarios.scenario:
Harrowgate Cold Storage is a fictional company that runs refrigerated warehouses. It is installing 4,000 small temperature sensors, a type of IoT device. IoT (Internet of Things) means everyday hardware with a network connection. The sensors sit on the same factory floor as the OT systems that run the compressors. OT (operational technology) means computers that control physical machinery. Each sensor reports readings over the internet to a cloud application that Harrowgate's developers build and release through a CI/CD pipeline. A CI/CD pipeline (continuous integration and continuous delivery) is an automated chain of steps that builds, tests and ships code every time a developer saves a change.

The vendor's first draft design has four weaknesses. First, every sensor shares one identical secret key that is written into the firmware. Firmware is the built-in software on a device, and a shared key in firmware means that anyone who extracts it from one stolen sensor can impersonate all 4,000. Second, the pipeline only runs unit tests, which check whether features work, and has no security checks. Third, the sensors sit on the same flat network as the compressor controllers. A flat network has no internal barriers, so one hacked sensor could reach the machinery. Fourth, when something goes wrong, an analyst must notice an alert and fix it by hand, which takes hours.

The security architect has listed the tools available. Mutual TLS (mTLS) is an encrypted connection in which both sides prove their identity with a certificate. A certificate is a digital ID card, signed by a trusted issuer called a certificate authority (CA), that binds a public key to a name. Only the matching private key, which must stay secret, can prove ownership. A secure element is a small tamper-resistant chip inside a device. It can generate and store a private key so that the key never leaves the chip, even if the device is opened. Revocation means the CA declares a certificate no longer trustworthy before it would normally expire. Code signing means attaching a digital signature to software so a device can check that the software came from Harrowgate and was not altered. A device should refuse to install anything whose signature fails.

For the pipeline, SAST (static application security testing) scans source code for insecure patterns without running it. SCA (software composition analysis) checks the third-party libraries a project uses for known vulnerabilities. It can also produce an SBOM (software bill of materials), which is a list of every component inside the software. Secrets scanning looks for passwords or keys accidentally committed to code. A security gate is a pipeline rule that stops a release when a check finds a serious problem.

For the network, segmentation means splitting a network into separate zones with controlled crossings between them. An IoT gateway is a device that collects traffic from many sensors and forwards only what is allowed. An allow-list rule permits only named traffic and blocks everything else.

For response, SOAR (security orchestration, automation and response) is a platform that runs playbooks. A playbook is a pre-written, step-by-step automated response to a specific kind of alert. A common mistake is letting a playbook take disruptive actions on OT, such as shutting down machinery, with no human approval. A wrong automated shutdown could spoil a warehouse full of food.

Your tasks:
1. Redesign how sensors prove their identity and protect data in transit, replacing the shared firmware key. Explain why your design limits damage if one sensor is stolen.
2. Name the security checks to add to the CI/CD pipeline. Say what each catches and how firmware updates should be protected before they reach sensors.
3. Describe how to restructure the network so a compromised sensor cannot reach the compressor controllers.
4. Outline a SOAR playbook for the alert 'a sensor certificate is being used from two locations at once', including where a human must approve.
modelAnswer: Give each sensor its own unique identity instead of one shared key. Each sensor generates its own private key inside a secure element, so the key never leaves the tamper-resistant chip. Harrowgate's certificate authority then issues each sensor its own certificate. Sensors connect to the cloud using mutual TLS. That means the cloud checks the sensor's certificate and the sensor checks the cloud's certificate, and all data in transit is encrypted. If one sensor is stolen, its key is hard to extract from the secure element. Even if the key were extracted, it identifies only that one sensor. Harrowgate revokes that single certificate, and the other 3,999 sensors keep working. With the old shared firmware key, one stolen device would have exposed every sensor.

Add SAST to scan Harrowgate's own source code for insecure coding patterns. Add SCA to find known vulnerabilities in third-party libraries and to produce an SBOM listing every component. Add secrets scanning to catch passwords or keys accidentally committed to code. Configure security gates so a serious finding stops the release instead of just logging a warning. Protect firmware updates with code signing: the pipeline signs each approved build, and each sensor checks the signature and refuses to install any update that is unsigned or has been altered.

Use segmentation to put the sensors in their own zone, separate from the zone that holds the compressor controllers, instead of one flat network. Sensors talk only to an IoT gateway. The gateway forwards only the needed reporting traffic out to the cloud application. Use allow-list rules so only that named traffic is permitted, and block everything else, including any path from the sensor zone to the OT controllers. A hacked sensor can then reach only the gateway, not the machinery.

Trigger: the same sensor certificate appears from two locations at once, which suggests the key or certificate was copied. Automated steps: enrich the alert with the sensor's ID, location and recent activity. Revoke the suspect certificate with the CA. Quarantine the sensor by blocking it at the IoT gateway. Open a ticket and notify the on-call analyst. Human approval point: any action that affects OT, such as changing or shutting down compressors, must wait for a person to approve it, because a wrong automated shutdown could spoil stored food. After the investigation, a technician re-issues a new certificate to the genuine sensor. This turns an hours-long manual response into minutes while keeping people in control of physical risk.

scenarios.title: Night Logins Through the VPN at Harbor Lane Logistics
scenarios.scenario:
You are the on-call security lead at Harbor Lane Logistics, a fictional shipping company with about 4,000 staff. At 07:30 on a Tuesday you are named incident commander. That is the single person who directs an incident response, assigns work to each team and approves urgent decisions.

A few terms first. Threat intelligence is information from outside your company about attackers: who they are, how they work and what traces they leave. An indicator of compromise (IOC) is one such trace, such as an internet address the attacker uses or a file fingerprint. A file fingerprint, called a hash, is a short code calculated from a file's exact contents. Two files with the same name can have different hashes, but two files with the same hash are effectively the same file. That is why a hash match is strong evidence and a name match is weak evidence.

This morning an ISAC sent a bulletin. An ISAC (information sharing and analysis center) is an industry group where member companies share threat intelligence. The bulletin says an attacker group is exploiting a known flaw in the model of remote-access VPN gateway that Harbor Lane uses. A VPN gateway is the device staff connect to from home to reach the internal network securely. The flaw is listed as CVE-2025-1111. A CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) entry is a public ID number for a known security flaw. The bulletin lists two IOCs: the internet address 203.0.113.45, and the hash A7F3 for a tool the attacker names svcupd.exe. It also says that after breaking into a gateway, the group logs in to internal servers at night using stolen service accounts. A service account is a non-human account that a program uses to run jobs, such as backups.

Your telemetry, meaning the data your own systems record about activity, shows the following. Your SIEM (security information and event management) collects logs from many systems in one place so they can be searched together and can raise alerts. It shows that VPN-GW-2 made outbound connections to 203.0.113.45 at 01:12 and 01:40. The SIEM also shows that the service account svc_backup logged in to file server FILE-SRV-07 at 01:55 from VPN-GW-2's internal address. Normally svc_backup logs in only from BACKUP-01, and only between 22:00 and 23:00.

Your EDR tool also has findings. EDR (endpoint detection and response) is software on each computer that records which programs run and can isolate the machine. To isolate a machine means to cut it off from the network while it stays powered on, so the contents of its memory are kept as evidence. On FILE-SRV-07, EDR found svcupd.exe with hash A7F3. On FILE-SRV-12, it found a file also named svcupd.exe, but with hash 9C21. That file was installed last month by Harbor Lane's own IT team as part of an approved update tool.

Your vulnerability scanner checks systems for known flaws. It reports the following. VPN-GW-1, VPN-GW-2 and VPN-GW-3 face the internet and are missing the fix for CVE-2025-1111. VPN-GW-4 and VPN-GW-5 are already fixed. The flaw has a CVSS score of 8.1. CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) is a 0 to 10 severity score based only on the technical traits of a flaw. It does not tell you whether attackers are actually using the flaw, or whether your system can be reached by them. The scanner also reports PRINT-SRV-01, an internal print server that cannot be reached from the internet. It has a different flaw scored 9.8, with no reports of attackers using it.

The network team owns the gateways and firewalls. The server team owns the file servers and service accounts. The service desk answers staff calls. The legal and communications team handles anything that must be reported or announced. Normal changes happen on Saturday nights. An emergency change can happen immediately if the incident commander approves it.

1. Correlate the threat intelligence with the telemetry. State which systems you treat as compromised and which you do not, giving the evidence for each.
2. As incident commander, give your first containment actions and assign each one to a team. Containment means stopping the attacker from spreading or continuing. Explain how you protect evidence while you do this.
3. Put the patching work in priority order, covering VPN-GW-1, VPN-GW-3 and PRINT-SRV-01, and justify why your order differs from simply sorting by CVSS score.
4. Propose one monitoring improvement for the SIEM so this pattern is caught faster next time, and say how you would keep it from producing too many false alarms. A false alarm, also called a false positive, is an alert on harmless activity.
modelAnswer: Compromised: VPN-GW-2. It contacted the IOC address 203.0.113.45 twice, it is missing the fix for the exploited flaw, and it was the source of the abnormal svc_backup login. FILE-SRV-07 is also compromised. EDR found svcupd.exe with hash A7F3, an exact IOC match. It also received a login from svc_backup at 01:55 from the gateway, which is the wrong source and outside the 22:00 to 23:00 window. That matches the bulletin's stolen-service-account behaviour. The svc_backup account itself should be treated as stolen. FILE-SRV-12 is not treated as compromised on current evidence. Its file only shares the name svcupd.exe, its hash 9C21 does not match, and IT installed it legitimately. A name match alone is weak evidence. It should still be included in the search for other signs. Treating FILE-SRV-12 as infected would waste effort and disrupt a healthy server. Missing FILE-SRV-07 would leave the attacker inside.

The incident commander approves emergency changes rather than waiting for Saturday. Network team: take VPN-GW-2 out of service, or block its traffic. Block 203.0.113.45 at the firewalls for all systems. Server team: use EDR to isolate FILE-SRV-07 instead of powering it off or wiping it. Disable svc_backup, issue a new credential and update the backup job to use it, then search the SIEM for any other logins by svc_backup or from VPN-GW-2. Service desk: expect calls about VPN access and the failed backup job, and give users a short agreed message. Legal and communications: inform early, so they can judge whether data on FILE-SRV-07 creates a duty to report. To protect evidence, isolate machines while they stay on, so memory is kept. Copy logs before making changes. Record every action with its time. Wiping or rebooting first would destroy the proof needed to learn what was taken.

First, patch VPN-GW-1 and VPN-GW-3 immediately as emergency changes. Patch the more critical one first, or limit access to both until they are fixed. VPN-GW-2 must be patched and rebuilt before it returns to service. PRINT-SRV-01 comes after, in the normal Saturday window. The reason is that CVSS describes only the flaw's technical traits. The gateways carry the lower score of 8.1, but attackers are actively using this exact flaw, the gateways face the internet, and one identical gateway has already been broken into. PRINT-SRV-01 scores 9.8, but it cannot be reached from the internet and nobody is reported to be using its flaw. Its real risk today is lower. Sorting by score alone would leave the actually targeted, exposed devices open longest.

Add a SIEM alert that fires when a service account logs in from an unexpected source system or outside its normal hours. An example is svc_backup logging in from anywhere other than BACKUP-01, or outside 22:00 to 23:00. Also load IOCs from the ISAC feed into the SIEM automatically, so any contact with listed addresses or hashes raises an alert. To limit false alarms, base each account's normal pattern on its real history, and list its expected source systems and hours. Match files by hash rather than by name, as the FILE-SRV-12 case shows. Remove old IOCs after a set period. Review the alerts for a short trial period and tune before turning on paging, so analysts do not start ignoring the alert.
